summary:
Oyo State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies in full to visitors, including the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the imprisonment terms it carries.

Oyo is governed by the Criminal Code, which penalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. These are the state-level offences a visitor in Oyo would be charged under, alongside the national statute.

Oyo lies outside the Shari'a regime. The death-penalty exposure for male same-sex conduct reported in twelve northern Nigerian states does not apply within Oyo, where secular penalties ceiling at imprisonment.

Police in Oyo profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay, a practice known locally as 'kito'. The extortion demand is the point of the stop in many accounts, and victims do not report it to police for fear of being arrested themselves or attacked.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk in Oyo. A BBC Africa Eye investigation broadcast on 15 May 2023 documented criminal gangs posing as potential dates on popular apps, luring men to meetings where they are filmed, then extorted, beaten and kidnapped; the investigation interviewed 21 people about being 'kito'd'. The underground scene it filmed was Lagos-based, but the risk applies to gay and transgender app users in Oyo as elsewhere in Nigeria.

No anti-discrimination protection is available in Oyo. LGBTI people there face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under a framework that reaches LGBTI organisations as well as individuals, and the practical effect is that reporting a crime or seeking help can expose the person who reports.
tangentialFactors:
The same framework produces recurring mass arrests at social venues across Nigeria: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a hotel raid in Delta in June 2018, 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023. These are raw counts from other states, ranked by volume only; they track population and venue size, and none of them is an Oyo figure.

The Shari'a regime that Oyo sits outside operates in twelve northern states, where male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death. A visitor moving north from Oyo crosses into that regime, and foreign travel advice warns of the death-penalty risk accordingly.

The BBC Africa Eye investigation also recorded enforcement against the extortion gangs themselves, including a police commander vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of officers arresting a kito suspect. That is a counter-signal to the picture of police as participants in the extortion, and it does not remove the arrest risk victims describe when they avoid reporting.
localsOnly:
Residents of Oyo who are perceived as gay face police profiling, entrapment and extortion on the street, with the demand for a bribe functioning as the outcome of the stop rather than any charge.

The 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations, so community organising, meetings and public visibility in Oyo carry imprisonment exposure for participants, not only for conduct.

Gross indecency, a three-year offence under the Criminal Code, is the charge of least gravity available to prosecutors in Oyo and the one most likely to be used where evidence of intercourse is thin.

Residents who are blackmailed or assaulted generally do not approach the police, because reporting identifies the victim under the same framework used against them.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Oyo-specific arrest, prosecution or violence incident appears in the sourced material. Every mass-arrest figure cited is from another state, and the dating-app investigation filmed its scene in Lagos; the application of that risk to Oyo is an inference from the national framework, not a documented Oyo event.

Whether the Oyo State police command has conducted or discontinued operations against perceived-gay people in Oyo is not sourced, and no Oyo court decision applying the Criminal Code or the 2014 statute is available here.

Access to HIV services, healthcare avoidance and corrections-placement questions for detained trans people are documented at national level only; no Oyo-specific data on any of them was identified.
